concepts.name: Energy quantization
concepts.statement: A quantized system can have only certain energies and not a continuum of them, which would be like a car that could travel only at certain speeds. This was the first break with classical physics.

concepts.name: Blackbody radiation
concepts.statement: An ideal radiator, a blackbody, emits a spectrum whose shape depends only on its temperature, and that shape could not be explained by classical physics. It was the curve of intensity against wavelength that gave the first clue that the energies of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Planck’s quantized oscillator energy
concepts.statement: Planck found that the atoms and molecules of a blackbody, treated as oscillators, could have only the energies $E = (n + \frac{1}{2})hf$. With this one assumption he described the measured blackbody spectrum correctly, and Planck’s constant $h$ entered physics.

concepts.name: Quantum energy step
concepts.statement: An oscillator of frequency $f$ can gain or lose energy only in discrete steps of size $hf$, much as a person on a staircase can stand only on the steps. Because $h$ is so small, these steps are far too small to notice in a macroscopic system.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.statement: In the classical limit of large, slow-moving objects, quantum mechanics gives the same results as classical physics. This is why quantization goes unnoticed in everyday life.

concepts.name: Quantized energies from atomic spectra
concepts.statement: A hot gas emits only certain wavelengths, a line spectrum, and if each emission carries an energy $\Delta E = hf$, the energies of the electrons in the emitting atoms must be quantized.

concepts.name: Quantized
concepts.statement: A physical quantity is quantized when it exists only with particular discrete values and not with every value in a continuum.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: A blackbody is an ideal radiator, one that can radiate equally well at all wavelengths.

concepts.name: Planck’s constant
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s is the constant that sets the size of the quantum steps of energy; Planck found its value by fitting his theory to the measured blackbody spectrum.

concepts.name: Atomic spectra
concepts.statement: Atomic spectra are the electromagnetic emission from atoms and molecules, which for a hot gas consists of only certain wavelengths.

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: When light strikes a material it can eject electrons, and the energy of those electrons can be measured with a retarding voltage. The details of this simple experiment are what forced Einstein to treat light itself as quantized.

concepts.name: Photon energy
concepts.statement: Einstein proposed that EM radiation is itself made of quanta, photons, each with an energy $E = hf$ proportional to its frequency. This is a quantization of the radiation, not only of the oscillators that emit it.

concepts.name: Properties of the photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: A threshold frequency below which no electrons leave however intense the light, ejection without delay, a number of electrons that grows with intensity and a maximum kinetic energy that does not: each of these follows from one photon meeting one electron, and several contradict a simple wave.

concepts.name: Einstein’s photoelectric equation
concepts.statement: The photon gives all its energy to one electron; part of it breaks the electron away from the material and the rest becomes the electron’s kinetic energy. This one line explains the photoelectric effect quantitatively, and its graph against frequency has Planck’s constant as its slope.

concepts.name: Photoelectric threshold
concepts.statement: A photon whose energy is less than the binding energy cannot free an electron at all, so each material has a threshold frequency $f_0 = \text{BE}/h$, and a longest wavelength, below which no electrons are ejected.

concepts.name: Finding a photon’s energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: We usually describe light by its wavelength, so you most often find the photon energy by combining $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$. With it you can compare any photon with the energies of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A photon is a quantum, or particle, of electromagnetic radiation.

concepts.name: Work function
concepts.statement: The binding energy, also called the work function, is the energy needed to eject an electron from a material.

concepts.name: Photon energies in electron volts
concepts.statement: On the scale of atoms the electron volt is the natural unit, and with $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s and $hc = 1240$ eV·nm a photon energy is found in one division.

concepts.name: Photon energy and radiation effects
concepts.statement: Because photons interact one at a time with individual atoms and molecules, what a kind of radiation can do depends on how the energy of one photon compares with molecular and atomic energies. This explains why UV sunburns and visible light does not, and why dyes fade in a particular order.

concepts.name: Ionizing photons
concepts.statement: A photon with more energy than the 10 to 1000 eV needed to ionize an atom can damage tissue on its own, so the high-frequency end of the spectrum is hazardous in a way the low-frequency end is not. The same energy makes these photons useful in medical imaging and cancer treatment.

concepts.name: Maximum x-ray photon energy
concepts.statement: An electron accelerated through a voltage $V$ gains an energy $qV$, and when it strikes the anode it can give all of it to a single photon. So an x-ray tube’s voltage in kilovolts is its highest photon energy in keV, which is how its penetrating power is adjusted.

concepts.name: X-ray tube spectrum
concepts.statement: The x-ray spectrum of a tube has two parts: a smooth distribution from electrons braking in the anode, and sharp peaks that belong to the anode material. The peaks, like the lines of atomic spectra, are one more sign that the energy levels of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Counting photons per second
concepts.statement: Power is energy per unit time, so dividing a source’s power by the energy of one photon gives the number of photons it emits each second. The enormous numbers that result show why individual photons go unnoticed in ordinary life.

concepts.name: Microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the band of electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about a millimeter to about a meter, below the infrared in photon energy.

concepts.name: Bremsstrahlung
concepts.statement: Bremsstrahlung, German for braking radiation, is the radiation produced when electrons are decelerated, as in the anode of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Characteristic x rays
concepts.statement: Characteristic x rays are x rays whose energies depend on the material they were produced in, appearing as sharp peaks in the spectrum of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Photon momentum
concepts.statement: Photons have no mass, yet they carry momentum, and a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ carries $p = h/\lambda$. This is why comet tails point away from the Sun and why a space sail could be pushed by sunlight.

concepts.name: Compton effect
concepts.statement: When an x-ray photon scatters from an electron, the two collide like particles, energy and momentum are both conserved, and the scattered photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength. This was among the earliest direct evidence that momentum is conserved in quantum mechanics.

concepts.name: Photon momentum and energy
concepts.statement: Setting the mass to zero in the relativistic relation between energy and momentum gives $E = pc$ for a photon, and with $E = hc/\lambda$ this is Compton’s $p = h/\lambda$ again. The two routes to the same momentum tie the chapter to special relativity.

concepts.name: Size of photon momentum
concepts.statement: Because $h$ is so small, the momentum of visible light is tiny, which is why mirrors do not recoil. It becomes important only for short-wavelength photons meeting light particles, as in Compton’s experiment, or for enormous numbers of photons with nothing to stop the recoil.

concepts.name: Applying momentum conservation to photons
concepts.statement: A photon absorbed gives its momentum to the absorber, and a photon reflected straight back gives twice its momentum. With these two facts you can find the recoil of a dust grain, a sail or a mirror.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of EM radiation
concepts.statement: Light shows interference, which is a property of waves, and it interacts as discrete photons, which is a property of particles. The duality is the name for having both, and the next question it raises is whether matter has it too.

concepts.name: Particle or wave in one observation
concepts.statement: The duality seems strange because the words wave and particle come from large objects, which never act like both. On the quantum level our observations reveal one set of properties or the other, but not both simultaneously.

concepts.name: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie proposed that every particle, with mass or without, has a wavelength $h/p$. It is the same relation as the photon’s, now applied to matter, and it opened the era in which quantum mechanics was founded.

concepts.name: Wave effects and obstacle size
concepts.statement: A wave must meet an object about as large as its wavelength to show interference, and a macroscopic body has a wavelength far smaller than anything known. This is why a bowling ball never diffracts and why the wave nature of matter was first seen with electrons.

concepts.name: Electron diffraction
concepts.statement: Davisson and Germer, and independently G. P. Thomson, scattered electrons from crystals and found diffraction patterns exactly consistent with the de Broglie wavelength. Interference is the hallmark of a wave, so these patterns showed that electrons are waves as well as particles.

concepts.name: Finding an electron’s speed and energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: With $p = mv$ for a nonrelativistic particle, the de Broglie wavelength gives the speed, $v = h/m\lambda$, and from it the kinetic energy. Check that the speed really is well below the speed of light.

concepts.name: Electron microscope
concepts.statement: Resolution is limited to about one wavelength, and electrons from a modest voltage have wavelengths far smaller than those of visible light. The transmission and scanning electron microscopes use this to see details as small as individual atoms.

concepts.name: Bragg equation
concepts.statement: Planes of atoms in a crystal act like the slits of a diffraction grating: electrons scattered from successive planes interfere constructively when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths. The same relation applies to x rays.

concepts.name: Probability distribution
concepts.statement: Each electron arrives at a definite place that cannot be predicted, yet many of them together build up a wave’s diffraction pattern. What quantum mechanics predicts is the probability of finding the particle at each location.

concepts.name: Measurement affecting the system
concepts.statement: A single electron at a time still builds up a double-slit pattern, so each electron interferes with itself. But if the slit it passes through is determined, the pattern becomes a single-slit one: measurement affects the system being observed.

concepts.name: Position-momentum uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: A probe short enough in wavelength to locate a particle well carries a large momentum and disturbs the particle’s momentum, so the two cannot both be known exactly. The product of their uncertainties can never be smaller than $h/4\pi$.

concepts.name: Energy-time uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Energy cannot be measured precisely in a short time, so a short-lived state has an uncertain energy. The spread in the decay energies of short-lived particles is used to find their lifetimes.

concepts.name: Finding a minimum uncertainty
concepts.statement: Using the equals sign in either form of the principle gives the smallest possible uncertainty, and $\Delta p = m\Delta v$ turns a momentum uncertainty into a velocity uncertainty. Compare the result with atomic energies to judge whether it matters.

concepts.name: Uncertainty for large objects
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant is so small that the limits the principle sets are far below anything that matters for a planet or a ball. This is the correspondence principle again, and it is why we never notice the uncertainty principle in everyday life.

concepts.name: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle sets a fundamental limit to the precision with which pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum or energy and time, can be measured together.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in position
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in position is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s position.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in momentum
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in momentum is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s momentum.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in energy
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in energy is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of energy.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in time
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in time is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of time, such as the lifetime of a state.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of all particles
concepts.statement: Every particle, massless like the photon or with mass like the electron, has a wavelength and behaves as a particle, and so do combinations of them such as nuclei, atoms and molecules. The duality is a universal attribute of nature, one more connection between matter and energy.

concepts.name: Classical limit of particle-wave duality
concepts.statement: A large combination of massive particles has a wave nature too small to observe, and a large combination of photons shows mostly wave behavior. This is why classical physics saw matter only as particles and light only as waves.

concepts.name: Solving an integrated photon problem
concepts.statement: A problem that joins photon energy and momentum to momentum conservation, heat transfer, circuits, wave optics or relativity is solved by identifying the physical principles involved and solving each part with the strategy of its own chapter.
